s: uses horse team [four-horse teams] The chariot race begins when the praetor releases four-horse teams from equally placed starting barriers. The poet supports the charioteer favored by the woman, worries when he loses ground, and urges the crowd to call for a restart. After the second start, the favored charioteer wins, while the poet says that his own desired prize remains to be won.

l: the speaker’s beloved woman, Heroides and Amores
s: The speaker’s beloved is a tall, handsome, fair woman with rosy cheeks, small feet, and star-like eyes. Though accused of false oaths, repeated deception, rejecting the speaker, and taking other lovers, she remains beautiful and apparently unpunished. Her beauty sustains the speaker’s love, drawing him back despite resentment from beginning to end.

l: the hard husband, Heroides and Amores
s: A husband relies on surveillance, placing a keeper over his wife; told her will cannot be guarded, he is advised to abandon sternness and indulge her friends.

is_a woman [whose chastity cannot be produced by force] The wife cannot be made faithful merely by having her body guarded, since her mind may remain unfaithful. Her beauty and the husband's concern for her make her more desirable to other men, and she may bring many friends into his social circle.

l: the white heifer, Heroides and Amores
s: The shining white female heifer, the bull’s consort in a dream, bears a crow-pecked dark breast mark, then leaves him for bulls in richer pasture.

is_a bull [the white heifer's consort] The bull is the white heifer's happy mate and lies beside her while resting and chewing. After the heifer hesitates and leaves him, he is left on the abandoned bed.

l: the nocturnal dream augur, Heroides and Amores
s: A nocturnal dream augur interprets the speaker’s dream, identifying the white heifer as the beloved girl, the bull as the speaker, the crow as an old procuress, and the dark mark as evidence of adultery.

l: the dream vision, Heroides and Amores
s: The dream vision shows a grove, a green meadow, a white heifer with her bull, and a crow that pecks the heifer before she joins other bulls. Its interpretation presents the scene as a sign of the speaker's love, the girl's departure, and adultery.
Perjury occurs when the faithless girl breaks an oath sworn by her own eyes and by the speaker's eyes. The speaker complains that her perjury remains unpunished and that he suffers for it instead.

Divine punishment is shown as falling on men and on figures such as Semele, while beautiful women who swear falsely appear protected. The speaker questions whether the gods exist or whether they favor tender beautiful women.

l: guardianship of women, Heroides and Amores
s: fails_to_control the wife's will [even when every door is shut] Guardianship of women is presented as ineffective because a keeper can guard the body but not the will. The speaker says that strict custody provokes wrongdoing and that indulgence is a better way to influence a wife.

is_a desire for what is denied Forbidden desire makes people strive for what is denied and covet what is forbidden, like a sick person longing for prohibited water. The speaker uses the horse, Argus, Danae, and Penelope to show that restriction can intensify desire, while permission can weaken it.
Anio, a river god, sees grieving Ilia by his waters, rescues her from the river, offers refuge among his many nymphs, and marries her.

l: crossing the river, Heroides and Amores
s: is_prevented_by the river's flood The crossing is difficult because the river has no bridge or boat and has grown far deeper than it was before. The narrator cannot reach the farther bank by any art and is forced to stand waiting.

l: Ilia's drowning and marriage to Anio, Heroides and Amores
s: is_a mythic episode Ilia throws herself into the rushing waters after declaring that she would rather have died before becoming publicly disgraced. Anio is said to place his hands beneath her breast, keep her afloat, and share the rights of marriage with her.

l: poetry and the liberal arts, Heroides and Amores
s: is_undervalued wealth and money [in the present age] The narrator asks whether anyone still respects the liberal arts or believes that delicate poetry brings any advantage. He contrasts poetic accomplishment with the military service and wealth that now win social preference.

l: the narrator's poems, Heroides and Amores
s: The narrator's poems please his lady-love, yet despite her praise, they leave him excluded outside her closed door.

l: the newly rich soldier, Heroides and Amores
s: A newly rich soldier gains wealth through bloodshed, joins the equestrian order, bears fighting scars, and is preferred to the narrator.

is_preferred_to poetry and the liberal arts [as a means of gaining wealth and status] War is treated as a more profitable pursuit than poetry because it can bring military rank and wealth. The narrator urges the wise to learn to follow battle and organize the foremost spears instead of merely producing good verse.

l: wealth and money, Heroides and Amores
s: Wealth and money are shown to control love, rank, public office, and social access. The narrator complains that those who can pay command his lady-love and that wealth gives weight to judges and status to knights.

is_a price [the price of Danae's seduction] Gold is described as more powerful than anything else because it can overcome resistance and purchase sexual access. The narrator also says that human beings dig gold from the earth instead of seeking agricultural abundance.
The poor, excluded from the Senate and money’s advantages, are denied love as the rich buy it; the narrator pleads for them to retain something to win.

The rich possess the Campus and Forum and control peace, war, public honors, judgment, and romantic access. The narrator allows them to keep these privileges but objects when their greed takes away the loves of the poor.

explores the sea [beyond what land requires] Human nature is portrayed as ingenious but harmful to itself. It creates fortified cities, weapons, sea travel, and the pursuit of wealth instead of remaining content with the land and its natural gifts.
Nemesis, Tibullus’s recent lover, mourns him at his funeral, kisses him, refuses to leave his pyre, and is imagined accompanying him in Elysium.
Delia, Tibullus’s first love and former beloved, mourns him at his funeral, kisses him with Nemesis and his family, and recalls being happily loved by him.
Bards are called sacred and the care of the gods, and some people believe that they possess divine power. Their work and poetic fame can survive death and fire.

Tibullus’s funeral includes his burning on a pyre and the attendance of his mother, sister, Delia, and Nemesis. His mother closes his dying eyes, his sister shares the grief, and Delia and Nemesis offer kisses before the pyre is left.

l: poetry and poetic fame, Heroides and Amores
s: Poetry uniquely survives the pyre, preserving Troy and enduring stories and ensuring Tibullus, Nemesis, and Delia remain known.
At Ceres’s annual festival, honoring Ceres and associated with Egyptian sistrum, the beloved must abstain and sleep separately; the speaker protests love, songs, and wine excluded.

l: grain and agriculture, Heroides and Amores
s: Ceres teaches grain’s cultivation, harvesting, and plowing with oxen and sickles, replacing acorns and turf herbs; when she leaves for love, crops fail except in fertile Crete.

l: Ovid's books of verse, Heroides and Amores
s: make_known Corinna [to many readers] Ovid's books of verse have made Corinna known beyond their private relationship. They have therefore helped turn her into a woman who may be shared with many and have harmed Ovid's interests.
Ovid's poetry, stirred by Corinna, publicizes her beauty and freely creates or transmits marvelous myths beyond historical truth.
Halaesus, exiled after Agamemnon’s killing, wanders land and sea, founds Falerii, and teaches its people Juno’s sacred rites.

is_founded_by Halaesus [with auspicious hand] Falerii is associated with an annual festival of Juno involving priestesses, games, processions, offerings, and animal sacrifices. Its Juno rites are said to have been brought by Halaesus, and Ovid wishes the goddess to remain friendly to Falerii and its people.

l: love affair and infidelity, Heroides and Amores
s: is_the_subject_of Ovid's poetry [in the elegies] Ovid fears that Corinna, formerly regarded as his own, is now involved with many men. He remains attached to her despite jealousy and asks her to continue her affairs privately rather than force him to know or witness them.

l: concealment and denial, Heroides and Amores
s: Concealment and denial protect public reputation and preserve Ovid’s peace of mind as Corinna is asked to deny visible infidelity, with words overcoming his eyes.

Ovid experiences sexual impotence with a beautiful and willing girl, despite her embraces, kisses, words, and efforts to arouse him. He wonders whether magic, poison, or shame has caused the failure, and contrasts it with his recent success with Chlide, Pitho, Libas, and Corinna.

His family had been of equestrian rank for several generations. Ovid's education was begun at Sulmo, and com- pleted at Rome and Athens. In deference to his father's wishes, he pursued, with his brother, the rhetorical studies usual with the ambitious young men of the time, expecting to enter upon a public career ; but so fervent was his passion for literature, and so irresistible his instinct for

; but so fervent was his passion for literature, and so irresistible his instinct for literary art — he himself says that whatever he attempted to write took the form of verse — that he found it impossible to follow the profession of his father's preference. He held, indeed, one or two minor offices in the public service, but his chief interests were always among the social and literary circles of the capital. Among those with whom he was intimate were Tibullus, who died when Ovid was twenty-four, Propertius, and Aemilius Macer of Verona. Horace and Virgil were his seniors by twenty-two and twenty-seven years respectively ; he heard the former recite, and says he

OVID'S LIFE At the age of nineteen, Ovid mourned the death of his only brother. The poet was three times married — twice with divorce as a hasty result, and the third time to a lady of one of the oldest and most respected families of Rome, the Fabii. The last union seems to have been based upon serious affection, or, at least, esteem, and remained un- broken to Ovid's death. A daughter, Perilla, is said to have been born of this marriage. In 8 a.d., the poet

is said to have been born of this marriage. In 8 a.d., the poet was suddenly banished by Augustus — with- out loss of property or citizenship, however — to Tomi, a distant town on the Black Sea, where he dragged out a miserable, though poetically pro- ductive, existence until his death in the year 18 at the age of sixty-one. The cause of his banishment is generally supposed to have had some connection with the scandalous conduct of the Emperor's granddaughter Julia. Ovid's literary activities began at about his twentieth year, and extended over a period of nearly forty years. His works fall naturally into three groups : the amatory poems, consisting of the

His works fall naturally into three groups : the amatory poems, consisting of the Amoves, the Heroides, De Medicaviine Faciei, Ars Amatoria, and Remedia Amoris, were the works of his youth ; in the following period appeared two poems, the Fasti and the Metamorphoses, which may be described as mythological ; and the final products of his pen, the Tristia and the Epistulae ex Panto, came from Tomi, and were in the nature of laments. Their language, nearly always artificial, frequently rhetorical, and often diffuse, is the same throughout — whether from the lips of barbarian Medea or Sappho the poetess. The heroin

whether from the lips of barbarian Medea or Sappho the poetess. The heroines and heroes who speak it are creatures from the world of legend, are not always warm flesh and blood, and rarely communicate their passions to us. The critic who cares more for the raising of a laugh than for the strict rendering of justice may with no great difficulty find room here for the exercise of his wit. Yet the malicious critic of the Heroides will be hard to find ; for they belong to the engaging sort of art which disarms criticism. Their theme, first of all, is the universal theme of love — and of woman's love — and of woman's love in straits. The

universal theme of love — and of woman's love — and of woman's love in straits. The heroines that speak to us from Ovid's page may lack in convincing quality, and may not stir our passions, but they are sufficiently real to win our sympathy, and to blind us for the moment to the faults of both themselves and their sponsor. Their language may be unvarying, and may border too much on the rhetorical, but it is full-flowing, clear, euphonious, and restful. It may be artificial, but its very artificiality is of charming quality. 8 IN APPRECIATION OF THE HEROIDES What the Heroides lose by reason of being the portrayal of legendary characters

HEROIDES What the Heroides lose by reason of being the portrayal of legendary characters in language removed from ordinary life they gain from their pleasant quality of style, and from their constant stimulation of literary reminiscence. They should not be judged as attempts at realistic art ; their author did not aim at even naturalism'. If we must choose, they should be judged on the basis of their connection rather with literature than with life. Yet we need not choose ; we may enjoy them as clever and genial treatments of literary themes enriched with enough of the warmly human to beget in the benevolent reader the illusion of life. Pene- lope, Briseis, Dido, and Helen no

reader the illusion of life. Pene- lope, Briseis, Dido, and Helen no doubt interest us mainly as figures from Homer and Virgil, but even they possess qualities that give them semblance of reality : Penelope is faithful, Briseis forgiving, Dido filled with despair, and Helen with vanity. In Medea, Hypsipyle, Oenone, and Ariadne, there is a nearer approach to real passion. The wifely solicitude of Laodamia, the loving trustfulness of deserted Phyllis, and the mother's grief of Canace are still more warm with life. The stories of Acontius and Cydippe, and in greater degree of Hero and Leander, are so full

and Cydippe, and in greater degree of Hero and Leander, are so full of the romance of young love that we think of neither life nor letters, but simply enjoy the delightful tale. And, whatever else may be said of his heroines, in every one of them the poet has placed the most human of qualities — a heart submissive to the power of love. All the world loves a lover, and all the world has for a long time loved most of the Heroides. P. Now are fields of corn where Troy once was, and soil made fertile with Phrygian blood waves rich with harvest ready for the sickle ; the half-buried bones of her heroes are struck by the curved share, and herbage hides from sight her ruined palaces. A victor, you are yet not here, nor am I let know what causes your delay, or in what part of the world hard-heartedly you hide. 59 Whoso turns to these shores of ours his stranger ship is plied with many a question ere he go away, and into his hand is given the sheet

We have sent to Pylos, the land of ancient Nestor, Neleus' son ; the word brought back from Pylos was nothing sure." We have sent to Sparta, too ; Sparta also could tell us nothing true. In what lands are you abiding, or where do you idly tarry ? Better for me, were the walls of Phoebus still standing in their place — ah me inconstant, 1 am wroth with the vows myself have made !
